solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

indicators.note: Cancelling the odd letters of 'tour' leaves only its even ones.

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of tOuR

explanation.surface: A government minister's earlier trip has been called off.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface minister is a politician; the definition wants a church minister. The 's is 'is', joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastor is a minister in charge of a Christian congregation.

parts.note: to taste something is to try it

explanation.surface: A small friend who has good taste.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little buddy' reads as a small friend, but 'Little' stands alone as the definition and 'taste' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Paltry means small or meagre, as in a paltry sum.

clue.text: Southern peninsula in part of modern Russia

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for south(ern)
Iberia is the peninsula holding Spain and Portugal

explanation.surface: A geography question about a southern peninsula somewhere within Russia.
explanation.walkthrough: The peninsula is not in Russia at all; 'in' merely links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Siberia is the vast Asian region of Russia.

clue.text: Seen in fog, really hideous monster

indicators.note: The answer can be seen inside the letters of 'fog, really'.

explanation.surface: A truly hideous monster looms out of the fog.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across the comma, from the end of 'fog' into 'really'.
explanation.definitionFit: An ogre is a hideous man-eating monster of folklore.

indicators.note: Reworking the word 'models' rearranges its letters.

explanation.surface: The models have barely been reworked at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very little' seems to describe how much reworking was done, but it is the definition, an adverb meaning rarely.
explanation.definitionFit: Seldom means rarely, so it happens very little.

clue.text: Stretch out with a gentle novel about love

indicators.note: 'Novel' means new, so the letters of 'a gentle' come out in a new order.

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, and zero looks like O

explanation.surface: Someone settles down for a long read of a gentle romance novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a book and 'love' like the romance's theme; one shuffles the letters, the other is just O.
explanation.definitionFit: To elongate is to stretch something out, making it longer.

clue.text: The same part of depot tidied up

indicators.note: In a down clue, going up reads the letters from bottom to top.
The letters are only part of the phrase 'depot tidied'.

explanation.surface: Same again: a section of the depot has been tidied up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tidied up' looks like one phrase, but 'up' is the reversal instruction for this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Ditto means the same as what was said before.

indicators.note: The bloke 'has' the time right after him, so the two pieces sit side by side.

parts.note: an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: A man finds he has time to go for a jog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run' looks like jogging, but it is the verb meaning to be in charge. Bloke is British for a man.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the business sense: whoever runs a shop is in charge of it, not jogging.

clue.text: Initial success as gnat, firstly, squished

indicators.note: A squished gnat is mangled, so its letters come out out of order.

explanation.surface: The day began well: first thing, a gnat got squashed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firstly' seems to ask for the G of gnat, but the whole word is fodder along with 'gnat'.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom from racing, where a runner already moving at the line gains an edge; figuratively, any promising first success.

indicators.note: Sprinkling scatters the letters of 'Braille' into a new order.

explanation.surface: A page covered in plenty of raised Braille dots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Generous sprinkling' reads as one phrase, but 'Generous' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of lavish or plentiful, as with a generous helping of sauce, not the political sense.

clue.text: Regularly concerned with all the Commandments, perhaps

parts.note: a story of love is one concerned with love
the number of Commandments Moses received; 'perhaps' admits the count is only one way to read the phrase

explanation.surface: Someone who regularly thinks about keeping every one of the Commandments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' is fair because ten is only one thing 'all the Commandments' could suggest.
explanation.definitionFit: Often means regularly, many times.

definitions.meaning: red as a lightly cooked steak is inside

explanation.walkthrough: 'Red' is an adjective for meat barely cooked, not the colour in general.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is steak barely cooked, still red inside; the other is uncommon, hardly ever encountered.

definitions.meaning: the two-note sound of a ringing bell
a noun here: a heated row or scrap, in informal British usage

explanation.surface: The boxing bell sounds and the referee calls for the fight to start.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a boxing match, and both halves of the clue belong to it: the bell's sound and the fight itself.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense imitates the chime of a bell; the other is British slang for a heated row or brawl.

clue.text: I am into Italian writer — sparkling stuff

indicators.note: 'I am' goes into the writer's name.

explanation.surface: A fan declares a love of an Italian writer's dazzling work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I am into' sounds like a fan's enthusiasm, but 'into' is a placement instruction, and the Divine Comedy's author is the writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Diamante is fabric or decoration covered in glittering imitation gems.

indicators.note: After a redesign, the letters of 'GP innovates' come out in a new order.

explanation.surface: A family doctor gets creative after giving a flag a new design.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flag' suggests a banner, but here it is a flagstone. GP is a general practitioner, a British family doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: A lesser-known sense: 'flag' is short for flagstone, the flat slab laid on pavements, nothing to do with banners.

clue.text: Far Eastern food, loads under chin in the end

indicators.note: Only the end of 'chin' is used.

explanation.surface: Slurping heaps of Asian noodles ends with food all down your chin.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'under' puts the loads below the N, so they come after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Noodles are a staple of Chinese and Japanese cooking.

definitions.meaning: a garment for the upper body; the British word here means a sweater
a flea is one example of an insect that leaps; 'perhaps' and '?' flag the example

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark and 'perhaps' flag that a flea is just one example of a jumper. In Britain a jumper is a sweater.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the British word for a sweater, a top; the other is a definition by example, since fleas are famous leapers.

parts.note: food that has gone off is rotten

explanation.surface: Someone is unhappy about a story's rotten ending.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' reads as an adjective in the surface, but as the definition it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym with 'Upset' as a verb: causing hurt feelings.

clue.text: Last metal: it gets processed after uranium

parts.note: U is the chemical symbol for uranium

indicators.note: Processing the letters of 'metal: it' reshapes them into a new order.

explanation.surface: The final metal to be processed in a nuclear plant, once the uranium is done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last' opens the clue as if describing the metal, but it is the definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the final one in a series, as in the closing chapter.

indicators.note: 'It' appears inside the word for bronze.

parts.note: a bronze skin colour is a tan

explanation.surface: The Colossus of Rhodes, a giant statue cast in bronze.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'bronze' the metal of the famous statue; here it is the colour, TAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Both name giants, from the Greek myths of huge gods and the huge statue at Rhodes.

definitions.meaning: bread baked as a single shaped unit
Cockney rhyming slang: the bread word that rhymes with head stands for it

explanation.walkthrough: Loaf for head comes from Cockney rhyming slang, loaf of bread = head; 'use your loaf' means think.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is a baked unit of bread; the other is Cockney rhyming slang, 'loaf of bread' rhyming with head.

definitions.meaning: in cricket, a set of six balls bowled from one end
an adjective: done, at an end

explanation.surface: Part of a cricket match has just finished.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one statement, but it splits into two definitions: the cricket term and 'finished'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cricket is played in sets of six balls from one bowler, each named by this word; the other sense is simply ended.

clue.text: Stage yet to be erected, back to front

indicators.note: Turning the phrase back to front reads its letters in reverse order.

parts.note: something yet to be erected is not up

explanation.surface: A theatre stage still hasn't been built and is facing the wrong way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stage' looks like a noun, a platform, but the definition is the verb: to stage a play.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrasal-verb synonym from the theatre: a company that mounts a production is staging it.

clue.text: Turn very morose in the end after sweetheart returns

indicators.note: The sweetheart returns, heading back the way it came, so it is written backwards.

parts.note: V is the standard abbreviation for very

indicators.note: Only the end letter of 'morose' is used.

explanation.surface: Someone becomes gloomy after their sweetheart finally comes back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn very morose' reads as 'become gloomy'; the definition is just 'Turn', meaning spin.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for turning about an axis, as a wheel or planet does.

definitions.meaning: a noun: a plant stem that spreads along the ground, as on a strawberry
someone who carries messages on foot

explanation.walkthrough: 'Shoot messenger' echoes 'don't shoot the messenger', but 'Shoot' is a noun: a plant's runner.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is a creeping stem sent out by plants like strawberries; the other is an errand-boy who carries messages.

parts.note: eras are times, periods of history
ED is the standard abbreviation for editor

explanation.walkthrough: 'Times editor' suggests the newspaper's editor, the one publishing this puzzle; 'Times' is just ERAS.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, as when pencil marks are rubbed off a page.
